newsitem.title: USA: Police investigate latest death linked to Kevorkian.
newsitem.headline: Police investigate latest death linked to Kevorkian.

text.p: Police Wednesday were investigating the death of another person linked to Dr. Jack Kevorkian's lawyer less than a week after the assisted suicide advocate burned a state order demanding that he stop practicing medicine without a license.

Police in the Detroit suburb of Romulus said the body of a 27-year-old woman from Indianapolis was discovered Tuesday night at the Relax Inn, near the Detroit Metropolitan Airport, after the hotel received an anonymous call.
A handwritten note found on the dresser said "Call Geoffrey Fieger," the attorney who represents Kevorkian.

Police would not release the woman's name. A spokeswoman at Fieger's office said he had left the country, but he told WWJ-Radio from an undisclosed location Wednesday that the woman was Heidi Azeltine, who was in the final stages of AIDS.

That would be the first AIDS patient linked to Kevorkian, the 68-year-old retired pathologist nicknamed "Dr. Death." As with three bodies found last month with notes referring authorities to him, Fieger refused to say whether Kevorkian was involved with the woman's death.

Kevorkian has not admitted assisting in a suicide since last November, when he publicly acknowleged being present at his 45th death since 1990. But Michigan officials last week issued a "cease and desist" order warning Kevorkian to stop practicing medicine without a license by helping people die.

He could face felony charges punishable by four years in jail and a $2,000 fine if found guilty of violating the order, which he burned publicly at a news conference April 4. His medical license was suspended in 1991 by the Michigan Department of Consumer and Industry Services.
Kevorkian is scheduled to go on trial in June in central Michigan for assisting in a suicide. He has been acquitted at three earlier trials on similar charges.

John Joanette, executive director of Friends Alliance, a Detroit support group run by HIV-positive people, said there was concern more people will chose to kill themselves before seeking out all the support mechanisms available to them.

Physician-assisted suicide in the AIDS community is not unusual, said Stephen Jamison, an adjunct professor at the University of California at San Francisco, who has written on death and dying issues.

He said he knew of many AIDS patients who have contacted Kevorkian, but he theorised Kevorkian had not been active in helping them die because there is already a strong underground network in the AIDS community able to secure lethal drugs.
